/Issued 1157 AM MDT Tue Aug 11 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

After weeks of hot and overall dry conditions a shift to a "cooler" 
and wetter, albeit short-lived, pattern is expected across the 
Northern Rockies from Wednesday through the end of the work week. 
High temperatures over this timeframe will fall some 10 to nearly 20 
degrees below normal as a cold front sags south from Canada, with 
multiple opportunities for rain, especially from Wednesday night 
through Thursday night. This Wednesday night through Thursday night 
timeframe remains the most favored for widespread rainfall, 
especially for areas along and north of the I-90 corridor. 

While most areas will see beneficial rains and cooler temperatures, 
the convective nature of activity on Wednesday and Thursday (most 
notably) may also bring a few strong thunderstorms with localized 
strong gusty winds, hail, and heavy rainfall capable of flooding 
normally flood prone areas (i.e. burn scars and urban areas). Areas 
along and south of the US Hwy 12 corridor on Wednesday will be at 
greatest risk of seeing strong outflow winds from collapsing showers 
and thunderstorms given inverted-V soundings, which is especially 
concerning given on-going wildfire activity across Southwest Montana 
in Beaverhead County.

Ridging aloft begins to build back in heading into the weekend, but 
another trough approaching from the Pacific NW will bring 
southwesterly flow aloft back to the Northern Rockies. This will 
result in temperatures warming back up, along with daily scattered 
shower and thunderstorm activity. - Moldan/RCG

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Increasing Chances for Rainfall from Wednesday through Friday...

Ensemble model guidance continues support multiple opportunities for 
showers and thunderstorms from the middle through end of the work 
week; with climate anomaly indicators suggesting that some of the 
showers and thunderstorms could produce periods of heavy rainfall. 
NAEFS analysis suggest that PWATs will climb above 1 standard 
deviation above normal by Wednesday evening across the Northern 
Rockies and remain so through Friday evening, with PWATS peaking as 
high as 2 standard deviations above normal during the day on Thursday 
across all of Southwest through North Central Montana. ECMWF EFIs on 
Wednesday support the potential for unusual rainfall amounts along 
and north of a Lewistown, to Great Falls, to Browning line with 
showers and thunderstorms; with the potential for unusual rainfall 
amounts (with respect to climatology) shifting south of the Montana 
Hwy 200 corridor on the day on Thursday.
